extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of poetics/drama
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating poetry (especially tragedy and epic): principles of imitation, plot construction (unity, complication/denouement), character, language, music, spectacle, and the use of probability and the marvelous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation: medium, objects, manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry (and allied arts) are modes of imitation which differ in three respects—the medium, the objects, and the manner or mode of imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which medium is used (rhythm, language, harmony), what objects are imitated (men in action of various moral types), and the manner (narration vs representation; combined or separate means). Examples: flute/lyre use harmony and rhythm; dancing uses rhythm alone; epic uses narration, tragedy uses representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (single whole)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy should be an imitation of a single, complete action with a beginning, middle, and end — a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plot must form a unitary whole such that its parts are necessary to the outcome; avoid disconnected incidents. The action's magnitude must be appropriate so the whole arouses catharsis without undue dilution or fragmentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot is primary (mythos)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot (mythos) is the soul of tragedy and more important than character, diction, or spectacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the arrangement of incidents so that the plot drives emotional effect and meaning; evaluate a work first by the coherence, necessity, and unity of its plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complication and Denouement (structure of plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots must include complication (dêlos) and denouement (lusis), with careful attention to especially the denouement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange incidents to produce logical progression toward resolution; ensure the denouement follows naturally and is satisfying, not ad hoc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex vs Simple Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex plots involve reversal (peripeteia) and recognition (anagnorisis); simple plots lack these and consist of mere change of fortune without discovery or reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer complex plots for richer catharsis when appropriate; use reversal and recognition in combination to heighten pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (Reversal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reversal is a change from one state of things to its opposite, producing a turning point in the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reversals that arise from probable and necessary causes within the plot (not arbitrary surprises). Reversal is most effective when tied to recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagnorisis (Recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge, especially about a person’s identity or other crucial fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design recognitions that are natural within the plot and that, ideally, coincide with reversal to maximize emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia / Error (cause of misfortune)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist’s error or frailty (hamartia) — an action or mistake — causes the reversal and misfortune, rather than sheer vice or depravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft the hero’s choices so that error is believable; the audience should feel pity and fear because misfortune comes from error, not from wholly wicked character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis (pity and fear)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy accomplishes a catharsis of pity and fear in the audience — the purging or purification of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the plot, characters, and incidents evoke and then cleanse pity and fear appropriately; the arrangement of incidents should culminate in catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (ethical fitness and consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be good, appropriate, consistent, and believable — neither wholly virtuous nor vicious for tragedy; character must accord with the action and probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure characters act in ways true to their moral type; avoid implausible deeds or sudden inexplicable moral shifts unless clearly motivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia) — intellectual content
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the intellectual element revealed in speeches (the themes, arguments and reasoning) and is part of tragedy’s persuasive/reflective content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express ideas and reasoning through speeches composed according to rhetoric; evaluate clarity, reasoning, and appropriateness of the lines of thought to characters and situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (lexis) and Poetic Diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction or language is the vehicle of representation; poetic diction includes choices of words, metaphors, and modes of speech admissible in poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance elevation with perspicuity; avoid making diction so brilliant that it obscures character or thought. Use metaphor effectively but appropriately to the genre and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody (melos / choral song)
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody (choral song and musical element) is an organic component of tragedy that contributes to its whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make choral odes integral to the action (not mere interludes); use music to enhance rather than distract from plot and emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (opsis) as accessory
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle (stage-visible effects, scenery, costumes) is an ingredient of tragedy but is the least artistic (more mechanical) element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle can produce pleasure but should not substitute for plot or character; do not rely on spectacle to mask weaknesses in plot or diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and Plausibility (poetic truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic truth differs from historical truth: a probable impossibility that serves art’s ends is preferable to an improbable possibility; the poet should prefer plausible presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer internal plausibility and necessity over factual realism; choose incidents that the audience can accept by poetic convention and internal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Wonderful (marvel) — use and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The wonderful is pleasing and may be admitted, but its scope varies: it has wider licence in epic than on the stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use marvelous elements sparingly on stage; in epic they pass without absurdity because they are narrated rather than shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid irrational incidents within the action
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrational incidents that are integral to the dramatic action (not external to it) are censurable unless there is inner necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If introducing an irrational element, make sure it lies outside the plot’s action or is made acceptable by strong poetic cause; do not rely on irrationality to salvage a weak plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of time and appropriate magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy attains its effect within stricter temporal and spatial limits than epic; the magnitude (length) must suit the single action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive length that dilutes unity; choose a temporal scope that keeps the action compact and coherent (epic’s long duration weakens unity on stage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin in the middle (sketch outline first)
rubrics_metrics.description: Start the narrative in the midst of action rather than with a long preface; sketch the bare outline of the action before filling in episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open at a point that allows immediate entrance into the action; outline to ensure episodes cohere and contribute to the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodes and episodic construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes (scenes) must be organized so that they are necessary parts of the action and not mere aggregates of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overcharge tragedy with epic-like details; ensure each episode serves the plot’s internal necessity and contributes to catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make Chorus and Dialogue organic
rubrics_metrics.description: Choral odes and dialogue must be organic parts of the whole, not extraneous ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate chorus into the dramatic causality and emotional movement; avoid choral passages that interrupt rather than advance the plot or character development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of metre and verse
rubrics_metrics.description: Different genres use different metres; metre contributes to genre identity but the imitation (not metre alone) makes the poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose metre suited to genre and effect; metre alone does not make a poem great—plot and imitation matter most.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing inappropriate elements from other genres
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not overload a tragedy with details proper to epic (lengthy narrative, irrelevant episodes) or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep genre-appropriate features: tragedy should not become epic in scope; maintain the specific ends and means of the chosen art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art’s end and audience refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: Each art should produce the specific pleasure proper to it; tragedy aims for intense, compact pleasure (catharsis) appealing to a cultured reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose with the end (emotional effect) in mind; adapt means (language, spectacle, music) to reach that end rather than merely to entertain superficially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth vs historical fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry states what is possible or probable and conveys universal truths rather than mere factual recounting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value what 'ought to be' or what is probative of general truth over strict factual accuracy; evaluate poetry by its capacity to reveal general human truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-types: better/worse/as they are
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation may portray men better than they are, worse than they are, or as they are; choice of type distinguishes kinds of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether characters will be elevated ideals, realistic portrayals, or degraded caricatures and keep portrayal consistent with the work’s moral and aesthetic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language elaboration in pauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Elaborated diction is suitable in pauses of action where thought and character are not expressed; otherwise it can obscure character and thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve ornate or highly crafted language for moments where it does not impede clarity of character or argument; use simpler diction in the flow of action and thought.
